Stockton-on-Tees' population increased by around 5,000 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 200,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Stockton-on-Tees increased by 2.6%, from just over 191,600 in 2011 to around 196,600 in 2021.

The population here increased by a greater percentage than the overall population of the North East (1.9%), but by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Stockton-on-Tees was home to around 6.8 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 6.7 in 2011. This area was close to the median population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Stockton-on-Tees than across the North East

Median age increased

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Stockton-on-Tees increased by two years, from 39 to 41 years of age.

This area had a slightly lower average (median) age than the North East as a whole in 2021 (42 years) but a slightly higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by just over 4,900 (an increase of 30.7%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by just over 3,500 (8.7% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 2.3 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Fewer couples without children

Stockton-on-Tees saw the North East's second-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of households including a couple but no children (from 18.6% in 2011 to 17.1% in 2021).

Across the region, only Northumberland saw a greater fall in the percentage of households including a couple but no children (from 21.0% to 19.0%).

Across the North East, the percentage of households including a couple but no children fell from 17.7% to 17.0%, while the percentage in nearby Hambleton fell from 21.3% to 20.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 1.5 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Stockton-on-Tees residents aged 16 years and over, 35.9% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 33.2% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in two people (45.6%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 47.7% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Stockton-on-Tees that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.3% to 9.5%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across the North East (3.7 percentage points, from 34.4% to 38.1%) than in Stockton-on-Tees (2.7 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Stockton-on-Tees increased by 2.7 percentage points

Change in housing in Stockton-on-Tees

Stockton-on-Tees saw the North East's second-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of households that owned their home (from 68.5% in 2011 to 66.2% in 2021).

Across the region, only County Durham saw a greater fall in the percentage of households that owned their home (from 65.8% to 62.5%).

Every local authority area across the North East saw a fall in the percentage of households that owned their home, as the regional percentage fell from 61.8% to 60.3%.

The rate of home ownership in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 2.3 percentage points

Disability in Stockton-on-Tees

In 2021, 9.1% of Stockton-on-Tees residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 10.4% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under one in nine people (11.0%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 10.7% in 2011. The proportion of Stockton-on-Tees residents who were not disabled increased from 78.9% to 79.8%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot was greater across the North East (1.8 percentage points, from 11.6% to 9.8%) than in Stockton-on-Tees (1.3 percentage points). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 1.3 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Stockton-on-Tees

In 2021, 4.6% of Stockton-on-Tees residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 3.5% in 2011. The 1.1 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the North East, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 2.9% to 3.7%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 92.0% of people in Stockton-on-Tees identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 94.6% in 2011), while 1.4% identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category (compared with 1.0% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category increased from 0.6% in 2011 to 1.1% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

Read the bulletin Ethnic group, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 4.6% of usual residents in Stockton-on-Tees identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category

Unpaid care in Stockton-on-Tees

In 2021, 4.2% of Stockton-on-Tees residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 6.6% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 40 people (2.3%) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.7% in 2011. The proportion of Stockton-on-Tees residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care increased from 3.1% to 3.4%.

This area had the region’s joint third lowest proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (alongside Hartlepool and Redcar and Cleveland). Across the region, only Middlesbrough (3.7%) and Newcastle upon Tyne (4.0%) had a lower proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 2.4 percentage points

Religion in Stockton-on-Tees

In 2021, 39.1% of Stockton-on-Tees residents reported having "No religion", up from 22.4% in 2011. The rise of 16.7 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Stockton-on-Tees. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the North East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 23.4% to 40.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 51.1% of people in Stockton-on-Tees described themselves as Christian (down from 68.2%), while 5.0% did not state their religion (down from 6.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 39.1% of usual residents in Stockton-on-Tees reported having "No religion"

Fall in employment

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in nearby Hambleton (4.7 percentage points) than in Stockton-on-Tees (1.2 percentage points).

In Stockton-on-Tees, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) decreased from 54.5% in 2011 to 53.3% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage in nearby Hambleton decreased from 60.0% to 55.3%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in Stockton-on-Tees fell from 5.2% to 3.3%, while the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were retired (economically inactive) increased from 21.8% to 23.4%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 1.2 percentage points

Stockton-on-Tees residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 180,500 Stockton-on-Tees residents said they were born in England. This represented 91.8% of the local population. The figure has risen from just under 178,400 in 2011, which at the time represented 93.1% of Stockton-on-Tees' population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just under 2,700 Stockton-on-Tees residents reporting this country of birth (1.4%). This figure was down from just under 3,100 in 2011, which at the time represented 1.6% of the population of Stockton-on-Tees.

The number of Stockton-on-Tees residents born in Pakistan rose from just under 1,200 in 2011 (0.6% of the local population) to just over 1,600 in 2021 (0.8%).

In 2021, 91.8% of Stockton-on-Tees residents reported their country of birth as England

Change in work hours

In Stockton-on-Tees, the percentage of long hours workers decreased from 10.8% in 2011 to 10.1% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage in nearby Hambleton decreased from 18.3% to 15.0%.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Stockton-on-Tees fell from 8.9% to 8.8%, while the percentage of adults in employment who worked 31 to 48 hours increased from 57.9% to 60.2%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 0.7 percentage points

Health in Stockton-on-Tees

In 2021, 45.7% of Stockton-on-Tees residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 43.8% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.1% to 33.7%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Stockton-on-Tees residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.5% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 5.4% to 4.9%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in good health in Stockton-on-Tees decreased by 0.4 percentage points

National identity in Stockton-on-Tees

In 2021, 3.1% of Stockton-on-Tees residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 2.2% in 2011.

In 2021, 0.7% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.3% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Stockton-on-Tees that identified as "British only" increased from 14.1% to 59.6%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the North East (1.1 percentage points, from 2.9% to 4.1%) than in Stockton-on-Tees (0.8 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Stockton-on-Tees increased by 0.8 percentage points
